source_text: Quae sunt ista, inquies, clausa atque obscura mysteria, quae nulli nec homines scire, nec ipsi, qui appellantur, dii mundi, parte queunt aliqua suspicionis atque opinationis attingere, nisi quos ipse dignatus est cognitionis tantae impertire muneribus, et in abditos recessus thesauri interioris inducere. Vides enim, si nollet inferri sibi a quoquam manus, summa illi fuisse contentione nitendum, ut hostes ab se suos, vel potestate inversa prohiberet? Qui caecis restituerat lumina, is efficere si deberet, non poterat caecos? qui debilibus integritatem, is debiles reddere difficultati habuit, aut labori? qui claudos faciebat incedere, is motus alligare membrorum nervorum duritia nesciebat? qui extrahebat a tumulis mortuos, huic arduum fuerat letum cui vellet indicere? Sed quia fieri ratio ea, quae fuerant destinata, poscebat: et hic in ipso mundo, nec modo quam gestum est alio, inaestimabilis illa atque incredibilis lenitas injurias in se hominum, puerilibus pro ineptiis ducens, manus in se porrigi ab immanibus passa est, durissimisque latronibus, nec reputandum putavit, quid illorum dissignasset audacia, dummodo suis ostenderet, quid ab sese expectare deberent. Cum enim de animarum periculis multa, mala de illarum contra insinuator, magister atque auctor, ad officiorum convenientium fines, suas leges et constituta direxit: non superbiae factum comminuit? non libidinum extinxit flammas? non hiatum compressit aviditatis? non tela extorsit e manibus, atque omnia seminaria totius vitiositatis abscidit? Ipse denique non lenis, non placidus, non accessu facilis, non familiaris affatu, non humanas miserias indolescens, omnes omnino crucibus et corporalibus affectos malis unica illa benignitate miseratus, reddidit et restituit sanitati?
pass_a_gloss: What are these, you will say, closed and obscure mysteries, which neither men nor those who are called gods of the world can know, nor can they attain to any suspicion or opinion, except those to whom He Himself has deigned to impart the gifts of such great knowledge and to lead into the hidden recesses of the inner treasure. For you see, if He did not want anyone to lay hands on Him, He would have had to strive with the greatest effort, so that He might prevent His enemies from approaching Him, or He would have had to use His power to prevent them. He who restored sight to the blind, could He not have made the blind unable to see? He who gave strength to the weak, did He have difficulty in making the strong weak, or in causing labor? He who made the lame walk, did He not know how to bind the movements of the limbs with hardness? He who raised the dead from their tombs, would it have been difficult for Him to inflict death on whomsoever He wished? But because reason demanded that what had been destined should come to pass, and He, in this very world, and not just as it was done elsewhere, with incomparable and incredible gentleness, considering the injuries of men against Him as childish foolishness, allowed His hands to be stretched out to Him by savage men, and to be handled by very harsh robbers, and He did not think it worth considering what audacity they had devised, as long as He showed them what they ought to expect from Him. For when, concerning the dangers of souls, He, the insinuator, teacher, and author of many evils against them, directed His laws and established rules for the limits of suitable duties, did He not break the act of pride? did He not extinguish the flames of lust? did He not restrain the gaping void of greed? did He not wrench the weapons from their hands, and cut off all the seedbeds of vice? He Himself, finally, not gentle, not placid, not easily approachable, not familiar in conversation, not unaware of human miseries, pitied all those afflicted with every kind of cross and bodily evil with that one benignity, and restored them to health.

pass_b_english: What are these mysteries, you ask, that are closed and obscure, beyond the understanding of humans and the so-called gods of the world? They are mysteries that no one can grasp, not even by suspicion or opinion, unless God Himself has chosen to impart the gift of knowledge and lead them into the hidden recesses of the inner treasure. For if God did not want anyone to lay hands on Him, He would have had to strive with the greatest effort to prevent His enemies from approaching Him, or He would have had to use His power to stop them. Consider this: God, who restored sight to the blind, could He not have made the blind unable to see? God, who gave strength to the weak, did He have difficulty making the strong weak, or causing labor? God, who made the lame walk, did He not know how to bind the movements of the limbs with hardness? God, who raised the dead from their tombs, would it have been difficult for Him to inflict death on whomsoever He wished? But because reason demanded that what had been destined should come to pass, God, in this very world, and not just as it was done elsewhere, with incomparable and incredible gentleness, considered the injuries of men against Him as childish foolishness, and allowed His hands to be stretched out to Him by savage men, and to be handled by very harsh robbers, without considering what audacity they had devised, as long as He showed them what they ought to expect from Him. For when God, the One who is the teacher and author of the laws concerning the dangers of souls, directed His laws and established rules for the limits of suitable duties, did He not break the act of pride, extinguish the flames of lust, restrain the gaping void of greed, and wrench the weapons from their hands, cutting off all the seedbeds of vice? God Himself, finally, not gentle, not placid, not easily approachable, not familiar in conversation, not unaware of human miseries, pitied all those afflicted with every kind of cross and bodily evil with that one benignity, and restored them to health.
